title: The Ferryman's Boy: Staten Island, the Isthmus, and the Iron Road to Forty-second Street
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Port Richmond, the birth on the north shore
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the house is reconstruction. No primary deed fixes the birthplace. New York Public Library researcher Andrew Wilson overlaid an 1884 map on a modern one and pinned the Harrison homestead to present-day 203-209 Port Richmond Avenue, which is the coordinate used here rather than the vaguer Staten Island pin found in the dossier.
stops.campa: On the north shore of Staten Island a son is born into a family that farms a little and works the water more, carrying produce and passengers across the Kill van Kull and down the bay to Manhattan. They name him Cornelius, after his father. More than a century and a half later a library researcher lays an 1884 map over a modern one and fixes the homestead where the birth happened to a lot on Port Richmond Avenue, a storefront now, a few doors from the Reformed Church. No deed names the house. The overlay and local memory are what the record has.
suggested_refs: NYPL Staten Island Stories, 'Finding Cornelius' (2016), on the map overlay locating the birth house
sources: New York Public Library blog, 'Staten Island Stories: Finding Cornelius' (19 July 2016)

stops.name: New Dorp, the Moravian baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested; the dossier tagged this as unverified report, wrongly. The NYPL Staten Island research blog gives the date, the officiant, the house, and the sponsors by name, so it is documented rather than merely traditional.
stops.campa: Six months old, he is carried to a baptism performed by the Rev. James Burkley, pastor of the Moravian congregation at New Dorp, not in the church but at the house of John Harrison. John Housemen, John Garretson and Phebe van der Bilt stand as sponsors. The Moravians are the family's people, plain and disciplined, and they keep their own burying ground on the hill above the village. He is buried in that ground in 1877, and his heirs buy the hillside beside it in the 1880s.
suggested_refs: The New Dorp Moravian congregation register and its burying ground on the hill
sources: New York Public Library blog, 'Staten Island Stories: Finding Cornelius' (19 July 2016)

stops.name: Whitehall Slip, the periauger
stops.date_confidence: year only, and the Manhattan landing is representative rather than documented: the slips used by periauger traffic shifted through the 1810s and 1820s, and Whitehall is the standard terminus for the period. Ownership of the first boat is disputed, see campa.
stops.campa: He quits the schoolroom at about eleven for the deck, and at sixteen he is working a flat-bottomed two-masted periauger between the Staten Island shore and the Manhattan slips, carrying market produce and passengers on the crossing. The story that he borrowed a hundred dollars from his mother and bought the boat outright hardens into legend after his death. A sketch printed while he is alive and prosperous says the boat belonged to his father and the boy worked it for a share of the profit. Nobody disputes the crossing itself, only the title to the hull. The two accounts have never been reconciled.
stops.quote: Until the age of sixteen, Mr. Vanderbilt was brought up on a small farm on Staten Island... commenced running a small sail boat between Staten Island and New York, which was owned by his father
stops.quote_source: 'The Steam Yacht North Star,' Scientific American, 18 June 1853
suggested_refs: Scientific American's 1853 biographical sketch, the earliest printed account of his beginnings
sources: NYC DOT, official history of the Staten Island Ferry

stops.name: The Narrows, provisioning the harbor forts
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the place. Sources describe harbor-wide wartime carrying and government contracts without naming a fort or a date; Fort Wadsworth is used here as the principal Staten Island defense point of the war and should be read as representative.
stops.campa: War with Britain fills New York harbor with garrisons that have to be fed, and he takes the government carrying work: provisions out to the posts around the Narrows, run at night when the wind serves and the naval traffic thins. It is the first money he makes that is not counted in single fares, and it comes from a government rather than a passenger. By the end of the war he owns an interest in more than one vessel. Which fort, which nights, on whose contract: no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: War of 1812 harbor defense works at the Narrows, supplied by contract boatmen
sources: general War of 1812 New York harbor defense literature

stops.name: Staten Island, marriage to Sophia Johnson
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the exact place of the ceremony is given only as the New York area in the sources consulted, so the family pin on Staten Island is used.
stops.campa: He marries Sophia Johnson, his first cousin, and brings her into a working household rather than a settled one. She will raise a large family, keep a hotel at a river landing while he is out on the water, and hold the marriage for nearly fifty-five years. What the record preserves of her in her own voice is almost nothing. What it preserves of her labor is a tavern's accounts, a passenger trade, and thirteen children who will one day contest their father's will. He is nineteen and she is eighteen.
suggested_refs: The Vanderbilt-Johnson cousin marriage of December 1813

stops.name: New Brunswick, captain of the Bellona
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia gives 24 November 1817 for his entering Thomas Gibbons's service.
stops.campa: Thomas Gibbons, a Georgia planter locked in a feud with Aaron Ogden, hires him to captain the steamboat between New Brunswick and New York in open defiance of the Fulton and Livingston monopoly, which holds by New York law that no steam vessel may enter the state's waters unlicensed. Vanderbilt runs the line anyway, dodging process servers, keeping the boat moving, cutting the fare until Ogden's passengers desert. He has given up his own sailing business for this, and with the wages he takes the running of the whole operation. He stays on the payroll twelve years.
suggested_refs: The steamboat Bellona and the Gibbons-Ogden feud over the New Brunswick run
sources: Hidden New Jersey, 'The Vanderbilts of New Brunswick'

stops.name: New York Harbor, the monopoly struck down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the decision. Vanderbilt was not a party to Gibbons v. Ogden and was not present at the Court; the stop is placed on the water he was actually working, not in Washington, per the rule that a stop belongs to whoever was there.
stops.campa: The case his employer brought reaches the Supreme Court, and the Court holds that navigation is commerce, that commerce among the states belongs to Congress, and that New York cannot license the water. Vanderbilt is not a party and is not in the room. He is on the deck of a boat that has been running illegally for six years and is now simply running. The ruling opens every river and sound in the country to anyone who can put an engine in a hull. He is thirty years old, and he has spent six of those years learning the trade from the man who paid for the lawsuit.
suggested_refs: Gibbons v. Ogden, 22 U.S. 1 (1824), the Commerce Clause decision that unlocked American steam navigation
sources: standard United States constitutional history of Gibbons v. Ogden

stops.name: New Brunswick, Bellona Hall and the end of wages
stops.date_confidence: year level. Gibbons died in 1826 and John Quincy Adams is recorded staying overnight at Bellona Hall that year; the departure from the Gibbons organization is dated 1829, and both are compressed into one stop here.
stops.campa: At the Raritan landing Sophia keeps Bellona Hall, the hostelry that feeds and beds passengers between the steamboat and the New York stage. The income is hers to earn and his to count, and in 1826 President John Quincy Adams passes a night under her roof on his way through. The same year Thomas Gibbons dies. Vanderbilt stays on with the son, William, for three years more, then takes his savings and his knowledge of the run and goes out on his own account, at thirty-five. He never works for another man again.
suggested_refs: Bellona Hall at the New Brunswick landing, kept by Sophia Vanderbilt
sources: Hidden New Jersey, 'The Vanderbilts of New Brunswick'
Vanderbilt family genealogy notes on the Bellona Hotel

segments.name: Fare Wars and the Move to Manhattan

stops.name: Albany, the Hudson pays him to leave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the practice and the year of the Hudson settlement; the Albany landing stands for the northern end of a route he worked over several seasons rather than a single dated visit.
stops.campa: He takes his brother's Peekskill line, extends it to Albany, and goes at the combination that holds the river with a fare cut to a dollar and then to nothing at all, taking his profit on the bar and the berths. The combination does the arithmetic and pays him to go away: money down and an annual retainer to keep off the Hudson for ten years. The arrangement is legal and printed in the newspapers, and he will run it again on Long Island Sound and on the Atlantic. He takes the money and goes.
suggested_refs: The 1834 Hudson River fare war and the buy-off agreement
sources: standard accounts of the Hudson River steamboat combinations

stops.name: Tompkinsville, the ferry he used to row
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year via the official Staten Island Ferry history. The dossier placed this at Port Richmond; that is wrong. The Richmond Turnpike Company's ferry, chartered by Daniel Tompkins in 1817 and running the steamboat Nautilus, operated from Tompkinsville on the East Shore, and the coordinate is corrected accordingly.
stops.campa: He buys control of the Richmond Turnpike Company, the concern Daniel Tompkins chartered in 1817 to run a road across Staten Island and a steam ferry from Tompkinsville to Manhattan. At forty-four he owns the crossing he used to work for other men's coppers. The Nautilus and her successors keep the schedule, the fares go to his account, and he holds the ferry until the Civil War years, when he sells it to his brother Jacob's Staten Island Railway. The island of his birth is now a line on his books.
suggested_refs: The Richmond Turnpike Company ferry from Tompkinsville, ancestor of the modern Staten Island Ferry
sources: NYC DOT / siferry.com, official Staten Island Ferry history

stops.name: 10 Washington Place, the merchant's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: lot purchased 1845, house completed 1846. Coordinate corrected from the dossier, which pinned Washington Square Park; the house stood on the block between Broadway and Mercer. Daytonian in Manhattan reports as settled fact that he had Sophia confined in an asylum over the move; T. J. Stiles calls the punitive version of that story false or badly distorted. Left unresolved here.
stops.campa: He buys a lot east of Washington Square and finishes a four-story house of red brick and brownstone at number 10, and the family leaves Staten Island for good. It is a merchant's house, not a palace; he will die in it thirty-one years later without ever building the marble his heirs build. Old New York money lives three streets away and does not receive him. Whether Sophia came willingly, and what it cost her to come, is the subject of a story that his biographers still argue about.
suggested_refs: Daytonian in Manhattan, 'The Lost Cornelius Vanderbilt I House, 10 Washington Place'
sources: T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009)

stops.name: Stonington, the first railroad
stops.date_confidence: attested for the presidency of the New York, Providence and Boston Railroad; the harbor pin stands for the Stonington line's terminus rather than a documented personal visit.
stops.campa: He becomes president of the New York, Providence and Boston Railroad, the Stonington line, having bought into its stock at a discount his own Sound steamers helped create. It is the first railroad he runs rather than raids. Passengers for Boston travel by water and rail together, and he starts to see the joints in that arrangement: where a boat hands passengers to a train, and where a rival's connection can be cut without anyone being able to sue about it. He is fifty-three years old.
suggested_refs: The Stonington line and the New York to Boston water-and-rail connection
sources: standard accounts of Long Island Sound steamboat competition

stops.name: Wall Street, the canal that was never dug
stops.date_confidence: sources split on the day: 26 August 1849 in some, 27 August in others, including Encyclopedia.com on the American Atlantic and Pacific Ship Canal Company. The concession went to that canal company; the Accessory Transit Company was the 1851 operating spin-off and is kept distinct. The stop is placed in New York, where the company was organized and where Vanderbilt was; the negotiation itself was Ephraim George Squier's, in Nicaragua.
stops.campa: Gold in California has made the crossing to the Pacific the most valuable route on earth, and Panama is neither short nor healthy. Vanderbilt organizes the American Atlantic and Pacific Ship Canal Company, and his agent Ephraim George Squier negotiates in Nicaragua a concession for a ship canal through the San Juan river and the lake. No canal is ever dug. What the paper buys instead is the right to move people across by river steamer, lake steamer and stage road, on a line some three hundred miles nearer New York than the isthmus of Panama. No record puts Vanderbilt himself on that river.
suggested_refs: The 1849 Nicaraguan concession to the American Atlantic and Pacific Ship Canal Company
sources: Smithsonian National Postal Museum, postal history of the Nicaragua route
Encyclopedia.com, 'American Atlantic and Pacific Ship Canal Company'

stops.name: Greytown, the Atlantic mouth of the transit
stops.date_confidence: route attested across postal-history and maritime sources; Vanderbilt's own presence at Greytown is not documented in anything consulted, so this is a stop on his line rather than a confirmed personal landing.
stops.campa: At San Juan del Norte, which the English call Greytown, the Atlantic steamers put their passengers ashore at the river mouth and the transit begins. Shallow-draft boats take them up the San Juan through rapids that no printed schedule has ever accounted for. The company's boats carry the names of the lake, the river and the man who owns them. By 1851 the Accessory Transit Company is moving thousands of people a month, and the fare war against the Panama route drives the price of a passage from about three hundred dollars down to about eighty.
suggested_refs: Greytown / San Juan del Norte, Atlantic terminus of the Accessory Transit Company
sources: Maritime Heritage Project, Nicaragua ports history
Smithsonian National Postal Museum, Nicaragua route postal history

stops.name: La Virgen and San Juan del Sur, the crossing
stops.date_confidence: route attested, personal presence not. Coordinate corrected: the dossier's Virgin Bay pin was in fact the inland town of Rivas. La Virgen, the transit port on the western shore of Lake Nicaragua, sits near 11.37, -85.77; the Pacific terminus at San Juan del Sur, some twelve miles further, is at 11.2529, -85.8703.
stops.campa: Lake steamers cross the freshwater sea to the landing at La Virgen, and from there a stage road of about twelve miles carries the passengers over the last ridge to San Juan del Sur, where the Pacific steamers are waiting for California. It is faster than Panama and cheaper than anything afloat. For six years the traffic of a continent crosses Nicaragua on a concession granted by a government sitting in Granada. The crossing costs each passenger mud, mules, fever, and a hotel bill at either end of it.
suggested_refs: The La Virgen landing and the stage road to San Juan del Sur, Pacific end of the transit
sources: Maritime Heritage Project, Nicaragua route description

stops.name: New York, the North Star sails
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: due out 19 May 1853, actually sailed 21 May, grounding briefly at Corlaers Hook, returning to New York 24 September.
stops.campa: He is fifty-eight and has never crossed the Atlantic. He has a steam yacht built at Jeremiah Simonson's yard, fits her out with a saloon of marble and satinwood and berths for his wife, his children and their families, hands the Nicaragua transit to associates for the season, and sails to Europe as a private man with no business to do there. The North Star is due out on the nineteenth of May. She leaves on the twenty-first, runs aground at Corlaers Hook, comes off on the tide, and stands out past Sandy Hook for Southampton.
stops.quote: He probably gives employment to more hands than any other one man in America
stops.quote_source: 'The Steam Yacht North Star,' Scientific American, 18 June 1853
suggested_refs: Jeremiah Simonson's yard and the building of the steam yacht North Star
sources: John Overton Choules, The Cruise of the Steam Yacht North Star (1854)
T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009)

stops.name: Southampton, the yacht nobody can place
stops.date_confidence: attested as the first major port of call; the month is from the voyage itinerary rather than a dated log entry.
stops.campa: The yacht makes Southampton and the English cannot classify her. No private person owns an ocean steamer. The Royal Navy sends officers aboard to look at her engines and the town comes down to the water to look at her hull, while the newspapers work out for their readers how a ferryman's boy from Staten Island came to own a vessel better appointed than a royal yacht. The Rev. John Overton Choules, sailing as the family's chaplain, is keeping notes that will be a book within the year. Then Vanderbilt takes the party inland to London.
suggested_refs: Choules, The Cruise of the Steam Yacht North Star (1854), the chaplain's account of the voyage
sources: T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009), excerpted at erenow.org
Vanderbilt New York, on the North Star voyage

stops.name: Kronstadt, the tsar's officers take her lines
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Russian call; Kronstadt, the naval anchorage serving Saint Petersburg, is used as the landmark coordinate because no source consulted specifies the berth.
stops.campa: She anchors in the naval water below Saint Petersburg, where the Russian fleet is fitting out for a war with Turkey that will begin within months. Officers come aboard with sketchbooks and take off her lines to be copied. The family is received ashore and the engines are examined below. Every courtesy is also a survey, and within a year Britain and France are at war with the fleet that took her measurements. He lets the officers draw. Whether he understood what the sketchbooks were for, or simply liked the attention, is not something the accounts of the visit settle.
suggested_refs: The Kronstadt anchorage and the Russian Baltic fleet of 1853
sources: T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009), erenow.org excerpt
Choules, The Cruise of the Steam Yacht North Star (1854)

stops.name: Constantinople, the Bosphorus before the war
stops.date_confidence: attested as a port of call, named in the full title of Choules's account and in Stiles; the month is inferred from the itinerary order.
stops.campa: The North Star comes up through the Dardanelles into the Bosphorus in the last weeks before the Crimean War opens, and the Sultan's officers come aboard alongside British naval men to look over the American ship. Choules records the visits, the coffee, the courtesies, the shore excursions of a family from Staten Island among mosques and caiques. Within a year these same waters are a supply line for an army and these same officers are burying men outside Sevastopol. Malta is the next call, where Royal Navy commanders tour her in their turn. Then the yacht takes on coal and turns west.
suggested_refs: Choules, The Cruise of the Steam Yacht North Star (1854), on the Ottoman reception
sources: T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009), erenow.org excerpt

stops.name: Saratoga Lake, the chip he did not order
stops.date_confidence: legend, disproven, and placed here to mark the alibi rather than a visit. The date is nominal, within the season the story claims. Vanderbilt was at sea or abroad from 21 May to 24 September 1853. Coordinate corrected: Wikipedia places Moon's Lake House on the bluff at 43.0559, -73.7295, some three kilometers from the dossier's pin.
stops.campa: The story told about him for a century and a half puts him this summer at Moon's Lake House above Saratoga Lake, sending his fried potatoes back to the kitchen as too thick until the cook George Crum slices them thin out of spite and invents the potato chip. He is not there. The complaining-diner detail traces to a potato chip trade group in the 1970s, and Crum's sister claimed the invention herself in 1899, when her brother was alive to hear it. The alibi is exact. From the twenty-first of May to the twenty-fourth of September he is at sea or in Europe, and the whole Saratoga season passes without him.
suggested_refs: Snopes and Smithsonian Magazine on the origin of the potato chip legend; Moon's Lake House, Saratoga Lake
sources: Albany Times Union, 'Vanderbilt helped invent potato chip in Saratoga? Likely a salty myth'
Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Curious History of the Potato Chip'

stops.name: Funchal, the last port before home
stops.date_confidence: attested as a call via the full title of Choules's 1854 book as catalogued by the Library of Congress; the date is inferred from the 24 September return. Note that most printings of the title name Italy explicitly, while the Library of Congress record (item 03011730) omits it.
stops.campa: Madeira is the last coaling stop before the westward run. Four months: England, Denmark, Russia, France, Spain, Italy, Malta, Turkey, and the Atlantic islands, the whole of it written up the following year by the Rev. John Overton Choules, who sailed as the family's chaplain and published the cruise as a book with the ports in the title. The yacht comes into New York on the twenty-fourth of September. Waiting on the pier is the news that the men he left running the Nicaragua transit have taken it away from him.
suggested_refs: Library of Congress catalog record 03011730 for Choules, The Cruise of the Steam Yacht North Star
sources: Choules, The Cruise of the Steam Yacht North Star (1854)
T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009)

segments.name: Transit War, the Atlantic, and a Ship for the Union

stops.name: Wall Street, the letter he may never have written
stops.date_confidence: attested for the coup: Charles Morgan and Cornelius K. Garrison restructured the Accessory Transit Company in his absence, per Stiles. The letter is not attested. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed; its earliest appearance is the New York Times obituary of 5 January 1877, no original is locatable, and every modern printing descends from that obituary. Wording here follows the canonical printed text.
stops.campa: Charles Morgan and Cornelius Garrison, left in charge of the Accessory Transit Company, have used the four months of his absence to reorganize it without him. He does not go to law. He puts steamers back on the route to bleed the line he built, and within four years the concern is broken and both men are out of it. The sentence he is said to have written them is the most quoted thing attributed to him. No archive holds it. It first appears in print in his obituary, twenty-four years after the coup.
stops.quote: Gentlemen: You have undertaken to cheat me. I won't sue you, for law is too slow. I'll ruin you.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to a letter to Charles Morgan and C. K. Garrison; first printed in 'Commodore Vanderbilt's Life,' New York Times, 5 January 1877, and classed as misattributed by Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Wikiquote, 'Cornelius Vanderbilt', Misattributed section, on the transmission of the ruin-you letter
sources: T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009)

stops.name: Le Havre, the European line
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1855 start via TheShipsList and GG Archives, which also give the end of transatlantic sailings as 1860, not 'around the start of the Civil War' as the dossier had it. The flagship pairing named in those sources is North Star and Admiral; Ariel, which the dossier listed, does not appear among the European line's ships.
stops.campa: He puts three or four ships on the New York run to Southampton and Havre, the North Star among them and the Admiral with her, and goes after the mail-subsidized Collins Line the way he went after the Hudson combination: better ships, lower fares, and no subsidy asked from Congress. He adds Bremen to the schedule later. The Collins Line loses two ships, then its subsidy, then its existence. In 1860, a year before the war, he takes his own vessels off the Atlantic and the European line ends.
suggested_refs: TheShipsList, 'Vanderbilt Line', on the New York to Southampton and Havre service, 1855-1860

stops.name: Nicaragua, the river taken back from Walker
stops.date_confidence: attested for the campaign and the seizure of the steamers; Vanderbilt directed it from New York and his personal presence in Nicaragua is not documented. The stop sits on his own transit line, where his boats and his agents were.
stops.campa: William Walker, the Tennessee filibuster who has made himself president of Nicaragua, revokes the transit charter and hands it to the men who took the company from Vanderbilt. Vanderbilt's answer is money and agents behind Costa Rica. Allied forces seize the lake and river steamers at their moorings, and the road that has been bringing Walker his recruits and his powder from the United States closes inside a week. Walker holds out into the next year and surrenders to a United States naval officer in May 1857. The transit never fully recovers.
suggested_refs: The Costa Rican river campaign of 1856-57 and the seizure of the transit steamers
sources: Western Cover Society, Nicaragua route postal history
T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009)

stops.name: Brooklyn Navy Yard, the ship given away
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date of transfer to the Navy; the location is reconstruction. No source consulted names the receiving yard, and Brooklyn is used as the standard New York naval receiving point of the period.
stops.campa: The Confederate ironclad has just destroyed two wooden warships in Hampton Roads and the government wants the fastest vessel in America. He gives it to them: the steamship Vanderbilt, by many judged the finest merchant ship afloat, handed over without payment. The Navy takes formal transfer in March and sends her hunting the commerce raider Alabama across the Atlantic and into the Indian Ocean. Lincoln reports the gift to Congress in July with an apology for not having mentioned it sooner.
stops.quote: I have inadvertently omitted so long to inform you that in March last Mr. Cornelius Vanderbilt, of New York, gratuitously presented to the United States the ocean steamer 'Vanderbilt,' by many esteemed the finest merchant ship in the world.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Lincoln, message to Congress, 17 July 1862, Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, vol. 5
suggested_refs: USS Vanderbilt's Alabama cruise, 1862-1863
sources: Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, vol. 5 (University of Michigan Digital Collections)

stops.name: New York, the thanks of Congress
stops.date_confidence: attested: joint resolution approved 28 January 1864, 13 Stat. 401. The resolution passed in Washington and Vanderbilt was in New York; the stop is placed where he was.
stops.campa: Congress votes him a gold medal for the ship, in a joint resolution approved on the twenty-eighth of January. The resolution thanks him for a gift to his imperiled country, actively employed in the service of the Republic against the rebel devastations of her commerce. The dies are cut by Salathiel Ellis and Emanuel Leutze. The language of the resolution is warmer than anything a newspaper has printed about him in forty years of public life. He is sixty-nine years old, and it is the only public honor of his life.
stops.quote: That the thanks of Congress be presented to Cornelius Vanderbilt for this unique manifestation of a fervid and large-souled patriotism.
stops.quote_source: Joint resolution of Congress approved 28 January 1864, 13 Stat. 401, reproduced in CRS Report RL30076
suggested_refs: CRS Report RL30076, 'Congressional Gold Medals, 1776-2016', for the text of 13 Stat. 401

stops.name: Wall Street, the Harlem corner
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia dates the corner episodes to 1863; older railroad histories cited in the dossier describe corners in both 1863 and 1864 and the two are frequently conflated. Not resolved here. The quote is from his testimony of 18 January 1867, four years later, and is given for the mentality rather than the moment.
stops.campa: He has been buying the stock of the New York and Harlem, a broken-down line nobody else wants, and takes its presidency. When the city council and a ring of brokers sell the stock short on the strength of killing his streetcar franchise, he buys every share in existence and then buys the shares that do not exist. The shorts must deliver, there is nothing to deliver, and they settle at his price. He does it twice. The second time, members of the state legislature are among the men caught short.
stops.quote: I would recommend them all to pursue the course that I pursue.
stops.quote_source: Cornelius Vanderbilt, testimony before the railroad committee of the New York State Assembly, 18 January 1867
suggested_refs: The Harlem Railroad corners and the New York street-railway franchise fight
sources: standard Wall Street financial history of the Harlem corners

stops.name: New York, word from Nice
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death, place and date. The cause is corrected: Find a Grave memorial 130329385 and genealogieonline record a lung disease contracted in Civil War service, not the malaria the dossier reported. A different George Washington Vanderbilt, born 1832, died in infancy in 1836; the son who died at Nice was born 10 April 1839. The stop is in New York because that is where his father was.
stops.campa: His youngest son George Washington Vanderbilt, West Point class of 1860, invalided out of the war with a disease of the lungs and sent to the Riviera to recover, dies at Nice on the last day of the year at twenty-four. He was born in 1839 and given the name of an older brother who had died in infancy. He was also the son the Commodore had picked: schooled, soldierly, sound. The one who will inherit everything is William Henry, whom his father has spent twenty years calling a blockhead and keeping on a farm on Staten Island. The father does not cross to France.
suggested_refs: Find a Grave memorial 130329385, George Washington Vanderbilt (1839-1863)

stops.name: Wall Street, the last ships sold
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year: control of the Hudson River Railroad acquired and the last vessels sold in 1864. The month is nominal.
stops.campa: He buys control of the Hudson River Railroad, whose track runs along the bank of the water he has worked since he was sixteen, and then he sells his ships. All of them. From this year on he owns rails and nothing that floats. The reasoning is on the map: a river freezes and a railroad does not; a boat lands at a pier, while a train can be run into the middle of a city and unloaded there. He is seventy years old, and he is beginning again in an industry he spent fifteen years raiding from the deck of a steamer.
suggested_refs: The 1864 purchase of the Hudson River Railroad and the sale of the Vanderbilt fleet

stops.name: East Albany, the bridge closed against the Central
stops.date_confidence: attested for the embargo and the January 1867 testimony that followed it. Vanderbilt directed the stoppage from New York; the stoppage itself happened at the river crossing at East Albany, which is where the pin sits.
stops.campa: The New York Central, which wants his Hudson River Railroad only in the months when the river carries freight of its own, breaks the through-traffic arrangement. In January he stops his trains at the river at East Albany and refuses to carry a single Central passenger or barrel across. A few days of it drains the Central's through business, the stock falls, and its directors come to him and hand him the road. Asked to account for himself before a committee of the state assembly, he does so without embarrassment.
stops.quote: It is not according to my mode of doing things to bring a suit against a man that I have the power in my own hands to punish.
stops.quote_source: Cornelius Vanderbilt, testimony before the railroad committee of the New York State Assembly, 18 January 1867
suggested_refs: The January 1867 Hudson River Railroad embargo and the Assembly railroad committee hearings
sources: T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009)

stops.name: New York, surety for Jefferson Davis
stops.date_confidence: attested: bond of $100,000 posted and accepted 13 May 1867, Vanderbilt among roughly twenty sureties. He did not travel to Richmond. Encyclopedia Virginia and the NYPL Digital Collections record that he sent his son-in-law Horace F. Clark to act for him while Greeley and Gerrit Smith appeared in person, so the stop is placed in New York.
stops.campa: Two years after the war he puts his name to the hundred-thousand-dollar bond that frees the former president of the Confederacy from his cell at Fort Monroe. Horace Greeley and Gerrit Smith sign in the Richmond court house in person and are hated at home for months afterward. Vanderbilt sends his son-in-law Horace F. Clark to sign for him and stays in New York. He gave the Union its best ship in 1862 and he stands bail for Jefferson Davis in 1867, and he explains neither one to anybody.
suggested_refs: FAU Digital Library, the Jefferson Davis bail bond of 13 May 1867, with its list of sureties
sources: FAU Digital Library, bail bond document

stops.name: Wall Street, the Erie War
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the mechanism; the month is nominal, the episode running through the spring of 1868.
stops.campa: He goes after the Erie Railway, the one trunk line into New York he does not hold, and buys its stock in the open market. Daniel Drew, Jay Gould and James Fisk Jr., sitting inside the company, answer by manufacturing more of it: convertible bonds turned into some hundred thousand fresh shares, fed to his brokers as fast as his money can take them up. He is buying paper printed faster than he can pay for it. The three cross to New Jersey with the proceeds. He never gets the road, and recovers most of his outlay in a settlement.
suggested_refs: The Erie War of 1868 and the convertible-bond issue that defeated the corner
sources: standard Gilded Age business history of the Erie War

stops.name: 10 Washington Place, Sophia's death
stops.date_confidence: attested. The asylum story attached to this marriage is reported as fact by Daytonian in Manhattan and rejected in its punitive form by T. J. Stiles; the contradiction is recorded, not settled.
stops.campa: Sophia Johnson Vanderbilt dies in the house on Washington Place after nearly fifty-five years of marriage; he is seventy-four. She had been his first cousin, the keeper of a river landing hotel in New Jersey, and the mother of thirteen children. Whether she also spent a season in an asylum because she would not leave Staten Island for Manhattan is a question two of his biographers answer in flat contradiction, and neither of them has the institutional record in hand.
suggested_refs: Daytonian in Manhattan and T. J. Stiles, in flat contradiction on the confinement of Sophia Vanderbilt
sources: T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009)

stops.name: Tecumseh House, London, Ontario
stops.date_confidence: attested for date, venue and officiant: 21 August 1869 at the Tecumseh House, the Rev. Dr. William Briggs officiating, per Wikipedia, WikiTree Crawford-4851 and the London Room digital collections. The dossier's claim that Braxton and Thomas Bragg attended as witnesses is corroborated by no independent source reached and is downgraded to reconstruction here.
stops.campa: He crosses into Canada at seventy-five and marries Frank Armstrong Crawford at a hotel in London, Ontario, the Rev. Dr. William Briggs officiating. She is thirty, a cousin of his own from Mobile, Alabama, and it is her kinship to the wife of Bishop Holland McTyeire that will shortly put a Methodist bishop in the Commodore's house and a university in Nashville. They tell New York afterward. The papers report a rumor of Confederate generals among the witnesses that nobody has since been able to confirm.
suggested_refs: London Room Digital Collections, the Vanderbilt-Crawford marriage record, London, Ontario

stops.name: Grand Central Depot, Forty-second Street
stops.date_confidence: attested for the depot: built September 1869 to October 1871 to John B. Snook's design. The consolidation is dated 1 November 1869 by the company's own annual reports and 1870 by Wikipedia; the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: The Harlem, the Hudson River and the New York Central are folded under one charter, and the consolidated system needs a single door into the city. He builds it at Forty-second Street, then the northern edge of settled town: Snook's shed of iron and glass, three railroads under one roof, opened in 1871. Passengers grumble about the walk from downtown. The city grows up around the building and then past it. In 1913 a larger terminal replaces it on the same ground and keeps the name.
suggested_refs: New York Almanack, '1871: The New Grand Central Depot at 42nd Street and Fourth Avenue'
sources: New York Central and Hudson River Railroad annual reports

segments.name: Gifts, the Will, and the Last Room

stops.name: 44 Broad Street, the lady brokers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the financing and the opening of Woodhull, Claflin and Co. on 5 February 1870; his own physical presence at the office is not documented in any source consulted, and is tagged as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Victoria Woodhull and her sister Tennessee Claflin open a brokerage at 44 Broad Street, the first firm on that street run by women, and the money behind it is his. The sisters are spiritualists and magnetic healers as well as brokers, and what passed between them and the old widower is reported everywhere and documented almost nowhere. Woodhull runs for president two years later. No source consulted puts him inside the office, on the stairs, or at the counter. The financing is not in doubt.
suggested_refs: Lower Manhattan Historical Association on Woodhull, Claflin and Co. at 44 Broad Street
sources: This Is Capitalism, on Woodhull and Claflin

stops.name: Church of the Strangers, Mercer Street
stops.date_confidence: attested: Deems founded the congregation in 1868, Vanderbilt bought the former Mercer Street Presbyterian church for him in 1870, and it opened as the Church of the Strangers on 2 October 1870. The price is disputed: vanderbilt.edu says $50,000, Daytonian in Manhattan says $100,000. Not resolved.
stops.campa: He buys the former Mercer Street Presbyterian church and hands it to the Rev. Charles Force Deems, whose congregation of newcomers and the unchurched has been meeting for two years without a building of its own. It opens as the Church of the Strangers on the second of October. Deems is a southerner who does not flatter him, and the first clergyman he has ever taken to. What the building cost him is disputed: one account says fifty thousand dollars, another a hundred thousand, and neither has been checked against the deed.
suggested_refs: Daytonian in Manhattan, 'The Lost Church of the Strangers'
sources: Vanderbilt University Libraries exhibition, 'Church of the Strangers'

stops.name: New York, the million for Nashville
stops.date_confidence: attested for March 1873 and the approximate million dollars, given as two separate gifts of $500,000 to Bishop McTyeire; Vanderbilt University's own history credits the founding gift to Cornelius and to his wife Frank Armstrong Crawford Vanderbilt. The quote is from his letter to McTyeire of December 1875, after the university opened, not from the 1873 gift, and the university's own short form of it drops two phrases.
stops.campa: Bishop Holland McTyeire, in New York for medical treatment and lodged in the Vanderbilt house through his wife's kinship to Frank, describes to the Commodore a Methodist university that the southern church cannot afford to finish. Vanderbilt gives five hundred thousand dollars, and then five hundred thousand more. The university's own history credits the founding gift to him and to Frank together. The school opens in Nashville in 1875 under his name and he never goes to see it. What he wants from it he sets down in a letter to the bishop that December.
stops.quote: ...if it shall through its influence, contribute, even in the smallest degree, to strengthening the ties which should exist between all geographical sections of our common country, I shall feel that it has accomplished one of the objects that led me to take an interest in it.
stops.quote_source: Cornelius Vanderbilt, letter to Bishop Holland N. McTyeire, December 1875, quoted at Vanderbilt University News, 'Women to the Rescue'
suggested_refs: Vanderbilt University, 'The Founders'; HMdb historical marker 214550, which dates the letter 2 December 1875
sources: Vanderbilt University News, 'Women to the Rescue' (2009)

stops.name: 10 Washington Place, the will
stops.date_confidence: attested: will dated 9 January 1875, its dispositive clauses reproduced from the probate and litigation record in American Heritage, 'The Commodore Left Two Sons' (April 1966).
stops.campa: He signs a will of a few pages that does the thing no American fortune has done before: it refuses to divide. The residue goes entire to one son, William Henry, the blockhead who turned out to be able to run a railroad. The daughters get incomes. The widow gets five hundred thousand dollars in government bonds and the house. Two years after his death eight of his children take it into court, and the contest runs a year and a half, with the autopsy findings and his physician's diary read aloud in open session.
stops.quote: All the rest, residue, and remainder of the property and estate, real and personal, of every description...I give devise, and bequeath unto my son, William H. Vanderbilt
stops.quote_source: Last Will and Testament of Cornelius Vanderbilt, 9 January 1875, reproduced in American Heritage, 'The Commodore Left Two Sons' (April 1966)
suggested_refs: American Heritage, 'The Commodore Left Two Sons' (April 1966), reproducing the will

stops.name: 10 Washington Place, the eight-month decline
stops.date_confidence: attested for date and place. Cause of death is contested: contemporary reporting said exhaustion from chronic disorders, while American Heritage, working from the autopsy and the will-contest medical testimony, identifies peritonitis as the immediate condition. Edward J. Renehan Jr., using Dr. Jared Linsly's diary, later argued for syphilis with neurological effects; Stiles rejects the stronger form of that claim. Left open.
stops.campa: He is eighty-two and has been dying since the previous spring, upstairs in the house on Washington Place, with reporters camped in the street and bulletins in the papers every morning. He receives visitors, gives orders about the railroad, and sings hymns with his wife and Dr. Deems at the bedside. The press calls it exhaustion from chronic disorders. The autopsy performed for the will contest finds peritonitis of several days' standing on top of everything else. What else was in him has been argued over ever since.
suggested_refs: American Heritage's synthesis of the autopsy record and the will-contest medical testimony
sources: T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009)

stops.name: Mercer Street, the funeral and the last crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested via contemporary newspaper coverage and the Daytonian history of the church; the route to the Battery is as reported in the press accounts.
stops.campa: The funeral is at Deems's church on Mercer Street, the building he bought and gave away seven years before. The pews hold the family that will spend the next two years suing one another over the will, and the street outside holds everybody else. Then the cortege goes down to the Battery and the coffin is carried aboard a ferry for the crossing to Staten Island, the crossing he first made for hire at sixteen, on a boat that may or may not have been his.
suggested_refs: 1877 newspaper coverage of the Vanderbilt funeral, indexed at iridetheharlemline.com
sources: Daytonian in Manhattan, 'The Lost Church of the Strangers'
Vanderbilt University Libraries, 'Church of the Strangers'

stops.name: Moravian Cemetery, New Dorp, the plain grave
stops.date_confidence: attested. The grand Vanderbilt mausoleum did not exist in 1877 and was not built until 1885-86, a distinction the dossier does not make explicit.
stops.campa: He is buried in the family plot in the old Moravian ground at New Dorp, on the hill above the village where he was carried to his baptism eighty-two years earlier, and a few miles from the shore where he first took money for a crossing. Sophia has been lying in the same ground since 1868. The grave is ordinary. Nothing on it would tell a stranger walking the rows which of these dead had owned the road into New York City. The mausoleum the name is now known by is not built until 1886.
suggested_refs: The old Moravian burying ground at New Dorp, first grave of the Commodore

stops.name: The hillside above New Dorp, the mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: attested: Hunt commissioned 1884, construction 1885-86 per Wikipedia and NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission Designation List 487 (LP-1208), reinterment 1888. Coordinate corrected from the dossier, whose pin fell about 1.5 km away in residential New Dorp; Wikipedia gives 40 deg 34' 48'' N, 74 deg 7' 00'' W. The model is the Romanesque abbey church of Saint-Gilles-du-Gard near Arles, not a church in Arles itself.
stops.campa: William Henry Vanderbilt buys the hillside adjoining the old Moravian ground and commissions Richard Morris Hunt to build a family tomb on it, modeled on the twelfth-century abbey church of Saint-Gilles-du-Gard near Arles, with Frederick Law Olmsted and his stepson John laying out the approaches and plantings. The ground is private and the gate stays shut. William dies in December 1885, before the work is done. In 1888 the Commodore, his parents, both his wives and his daughter Frances are lifted out of the old burying ground and carried up the hill into it. New York City designates the tomb a landmark in 2016.
suggested_refs: Library of Congress item 2017645655, Hunt's rendering of the mausoleum facade; Olmsted Online job record 00218
sources: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, Designation List 487, LP-1208 (2016)
Vanderbilt Cup Races blog, 'Mystery Foto #45 Solved'

stops.name: Grand Central Terminal, the statue moved
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1869 bronze and its 1929 relocation. Sculptor corrected: the work is Ernst Plassmann's, long misattributed to Albert De Groot until David M. Kahn corrected the record in The Connoisseur, June 1980. The dossier left the relocation year open between 1913 and 1929; Wikipedia's 'Grand Central Terminal art' and 'Ernst Plassmann' both give 1929.
stops.campa: The bronze Ernst Plassmann casts of him in 1869, eight and a half feet of Commodore in a fur-collared coat, stands at the center of a hundred-and-fifty-foot relief on his own freight depot at St. John's Park, a monument he pays for himself and stands under at its unveiling. The depot comes down and the relief is broken up. The figure alone survives it. In 1929 it is set on the south face of Grand Central Terminal, above the viaduct that carries Park Avenue around the building.
suggested_refs: Dianne L. Durante on the Plassmann bronze at Grand Central; Jules-Felix Coutan's 'Glory of Commerce' group of 1914, mounted on the same south facade above it
sources: Dianne L. Durante, 'Cornelius Vanderbilt by Ernst Plassmann, Grand Central Terminal'

stops.name: Vanderbilt University, the medal comes back
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2022 donation via the Vanderbilt University Libraries exhibition 'Gifts of Gold for the Commodore'; the month is nominal, the exhibition giving autumn 2022. He never visited Nashville in his life.
stops.campa: The gold medal Congress voted him for the ship stays in the family for a hundred and fifty-eight years. In 2010 the biography that reframed him as a builder of the corporation rather than a robber baron takes the Pulitzer. In the autumn of 2022 the descendants of William Henry Vanderbilt give the medal to the university in Nashville that he paid for and never saw. It goes into the memorabilia collection, a short walk from the athletic teams still called the Commodores, after a steamboat nickname a man earned on the Hudson before the Civil War.
suggested_refs: Vanderbilt University Libraries exhibition, 'Gifts of Gold for the Commodore'; T. J. Stiles, The First Tycoon (2009), Pulitzer Prize for Biography 2010
sources: Vanderbilt University Libraries, 'Gifts of Gold for the Commodore'
